title: Chapter 6 Drill: Colon, Rectum, Anus, and the Abdominal Wall

items.stem: During a left colectomy for a descending colon cancer, a surgeon mobilizes the colon medially to laterally off the retroperitoneum. Which structure, lying on the psoas fascia beneath the mesocolon and crossing the iliac bifurcation, is most important to identify and protect?
options: The left ureter
The left gonadal vein as the main structure of concern
The genitofemoral nerve running with the inferior mesenteric vein
The left common iliac artery anterior to the sigmoid mesocolon
items.explanation: The left ureter lies in the retroperitoneum on the psoas, crosses the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, and is the structure whose unrecognized injury causes serious morbidity. The gonadal vein runs near it but injury is minor. The genitofemoral nerve lies on the psoas muscle, not with the mesenteric vein. The iliac artery lies deeper and is not routinely exposed by this plane.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man completed resection and adjuvant therapy for stage III colon cancer. A colonoscopy was complete before surgery. Which surveillance plan is the most appropriate?
options: Whole-body PET-CT every 3 months for 5 years, with no carcinoembryonic antigen or colonoscopy follow-up
Carcinoembryonic antigen every 3 to 6 months for 2 years, periodic CT, and colonoscopy at 1 year
No scheduled testing unless symptoms develop
Annual pelvic MRI and stool testing at home without colonoscopy
items.explanation: After curative treatment of stage III disease, guidelines recommend serial carcinoembryonic antigen measurement, periodic cross-sectional imaging, and a colonoscopy about a year after resection, with repeat intervals based on findings. Frequent PET adds radiation and false positives without proven survival benefit. Waiting for symptoms misses resectable recurrence, and pelvic MRI with stool testing does not replace endoscopy.

items.stem: A 52-year-old otherwise fit woman has a full-thickness rectal prolapse and long-standing constipation. She wants a durable repair. Which operation is the most appropriate?
options: Perineal mucosal sleeve resection without any fixation to the sacrum
Anal encirclement with a Thiersch wire
Hemorrhoid banding to reduce the prolapsing tissue
Abdominal rectopexy with sigmoid resection, given her constipation
items.explanation: A fit patient with rectal prolapse is best treated by an abdominal approach, which has lower recurrence than perineal procedures. When constipation is prominent, adding sigmoid resection to rectopexy treats the redundant colon and reduces postoperative constipation. Perineal approaches suit frail patients. A Thiersch wire is rarely used and has high failure. Banding does not treat full-thickness prolapse.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted with profound hypotension from a urinary source of sepsis. On day 2 she has crampy left-sided abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Colonoscopy shows patchy pale, edematous mucosa with linear ulcers at the splenic flexure, and the rectum looks normal. Which explanation best accounts for the distribution of injury?
options: Occlusion of the ileocolic artery by an embolus from the left atrium
Venous thrombosis of the inferior mesenteric vein draining the descending colon
A watershed zone where the superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories meet through a sometimes thin marginal artery
Direct bacterial invasion of the left colonic mucosa by enteric pathogens
items.explanation: The splenic flexure sits where the superior and inferior mesenteric territories meet, and the marginal artery there can be diminutive, so low flow injures it first. The rectum is spared because of its dual supply from internal iliac branches. An ileocolic embolus would injure the right colon. Isolated inferior mesenteric vein thrombosis is rare, and infectious colitis does not give this pale, segmental pattern after shock.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man has a pedunculated colon polyp with a 1.5 cm head removed completely by snare polypectomy. Pathology shows adenocarcinoma invading the submucosa of the stalk only, well differentiated, with no lymphovascular invasion and a margin of 3 mm. What is the best management?
options: Segmental colectomy with lymph node dissection
Endoscopic surveillance alone, since the favorable features and clear margin make polypectomy sufficient
Adjuvant chemotherapy followed by repeat colonoscopy
Completion polypectomy site tattoo and PET imaging
items.explanation: A malignant pedunculated polyp with favorable pathology has a low nodal risk, so complete excision is adequate. Those features are well or moderate differentiation, no lymphovascular invasion, a margin of at least 1 to 2 mm, and no budding. Colectomy is reserved for unfavorable features. Chemotherapy has no role in T1 disease with good histology. Surveillance should include a site check at about 3 to 6 months.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man has had ulcerative colitis for 16 years. Surveillance colonoscopy shows no visible lesion, but random biopsies from the transverse colon show high-grade dysplasia, confirmed by a second pathologist. He is well and in remission. What is the best recommendation?
options: Total proctocolectomy, with an ileal pouch if suitable
Repeat colonoscopy in 3 months with random biopsies
Segmental right colectomy of the dysplastic segment only
Intensify mesalamine and repeat surveillance in 1 year
items.explanation: Flat high-grade dysplasia in long-standing colitis carries a high risk of existing or imminent cancer, and the whole mucosa is at risk. Total proctocolectomy removes all at-risk epithelium and permits pouch reconstruction. Segmental resection leaves diseased mucosa that may develop cancer. Short interval repeat surveillance and medical therapy are not adequate for confirmed high-grade dysplasia.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman notices a midline ridge above and below the umbilicus when she sits up, beginning after her second pregnancy. She has no pain. Examination shows a soft bulge during contraction, and ultrasound shows widened rectus muscles with intact linea alba. What is the best management?
options: Urgent laparoscopic repair with intraperitoneal mesh placement for the defect
Open primary fascial repair of the linea alba
Reassurance and physical therapy, as this is diastasis recti, not a hernia
CT-guided biopsy of the linea alba
items.explanation: Diastasis recti is a widening of the rectus muscles with an intact linea alba, common after pregnancy, and it contains no hernia sac and carries no risk of incarceration. Management is reassurance and core strengthening, and surgery is reserved for cosmetic or functional indications after other options. Urgent repair, open fascial repair, and biopsy are unnecessary.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man undergoes appendectomy for suspected acute appendicitis. Pathology shows adenocarcinoma of the appendix, 1.8 cm, invading the subserosa, with a tumor-free resection margin and no mucin. CT afterward shows no distant disease. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Observation with annual colonoscopy only
Completion cecectomy with a small ileal margin
Systemic chemotherapy alone without further resection
Right hemicolectomy with regional lymphadenectomy
items.explanation: Invasive appendiceal adenocarcinoma beyond the mucosa has meaningful nodal risk, so oncologic resection by right hemicolectomy is recommended. Appendectomy alone leaves regional nodes unstaged. Cecectomy gives no nodal sampling. Chemotherapy alone does not replace resection in localized disease. Observation is acceptable only for small low-grade noninvasive lesions confined to the appendix, and this tumor invades beyond the mucosa.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has a sigmoid adenocarcinoma with multiple unresectable liver and lung metastases. He has no bleeding, obstruction, or perforation and has good performance status. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Palliative sigmoid colectomy before any chemotherapy
Systemic chemotherapy first, without resection of the primary
Diverting loop colostomy to prevent future obstruction
Radiation of the primary followed by total mesorectal excision
items.explanation: In unresectable stage IV colorectal cancer, the primary tumor rarely causes complications, and trials show no survival benefit from upfront resection. Systemic therapy is therefore started first, and surgery is reserved for obstruction, perforation, or bleeding. Prophylactic colostomy exposes the patient to stoma risks without need. Chemoradiation and total mesorectal excision apply to rectal cancer and do not fit a sigmoid primary.

items.stem: During laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair, a surgeon plans to fix mesh with tacks. Which anatomic area lateral to the gonadal vessels and below the iliopubic tract should be avoided because of the risk of nerve entrapment and chronic pain?
options: The triangle of pain, holding the femoral cutaneous and genitofemoral nerves
The triangle of doom, bounded medially by the vas deferens and laterally by the gonadal vessels
The area of the pubic tubercle with Cooper ligament
The area medial to the inferior epigastric vessels
items.explanation: The triangle of pain lies lateral to the gonadal vessels and below the iliopubic tract and holds the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve, so tacks there can cause chronic neuralgia. The triangle of doom, bounded by the vas and gonadal vessels, holds the iliac vessels. Fixation to Cooper ligament is standard, and the region medial to the epigastric vessels is safe.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has a transsphincteric anal fistula that crosses about 70 percent of the external sphincter. Fistulotomy would likely cause incontinence. He has no Crohn disease. Which initial surgical approach best preserves continence?
options: Primary fistulotomy dividing all of the involved sphincter
Repeated incision of the external opening only
Fibrin glue as the only definitive treatment
Placement of a draining seton, with later sphincter-sparing repair such as ligation of the intersphincteric tract
items.explanation: High transsphincteric fistulas involve a large share of the sphincter, so cutting through them risks incontinence. A draining seton controls sepsis and matures the tract, and a sphincter-sparing procedure such as ligation of the intersphincteric tract or an advancement flap can follow. Repeated incision of the external opening does not address the tract. Fibrin glue has low success and is not definitive.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has a symptomatic 3 cm umbilical hernia with a body mass index of 31. He has no ascites or wound infection. Which repair is best for lowering recurrence?
options: Primary suture repair, as mesh adds only infection risk
Observation until the hernia incarcerates
Mesh repair, because defects larger than about 1 to 2 cm have lower recurrence with mesh than with suture
Component separation with a bridged biologic mesh
items.explanation: For umbilical and small ventral hernias, randomized evidence shows that mesh reduces recurrence compared with suture repair, especially when the defect is larger than 1 to 2 cm or the patient is obese. Suture repair remains acceptable for very small defects. Waiting for incarceration raises emergency risk. Component separation and bridging biologic mesh are too extensive for a 3 cm defect.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has an 8 cm incisional hernia after hysterectomy. The abdomen is clean and she has quit smoking. The surgeon plans an open repair with synthetic mesh. Which mesh position and closure give the lowest recurrence and wound complication rates?
options: Onlay mesh placed on the anterior fascia over the defect
Retromuscular sublay mesh with the anterior fascia closed over it
Intraperitoneal mesh bridging the open defect
Primary fascial suture of the defect without any mesh reinforcement at all
items.explanation: Sublay placement in the retromuscular plane, with the fascial defect closed over the mesh, gives good mesh incorporation, protects against bowel contact, and has low recurrence and infection rates. Onlay mesh sits in the subcutaneous plane with more seroma and infection. Bridging leaves a gap and recurs more often. Suture alone fails in large defects.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has one 12 mm tubulovillous adenoma removed completely at colonoscopy. The preparation was excellent and no other polyps were found. She has no family history of colorectal cancer. When should her next surveillance colonoscopy be scheduled?
options: In 3 years, because an advanced adenoma was found
In 10 years, as for an average-risk patient
In 1 year, because of villous histology
In 5 years, because only one polyp was found
items.explanation: An adenoma of at least 10 mm or with villous features is advanced, and current multisociety guidance recommends repeat colonoscopy in 3 years after complete removal. A 10-year interval applies to a normal examination. One year is reserved for more than 10 adenomas or piecemeal resection of large lesions. Five years fits only one or two small tubular adenomas.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man has a 1.5 cm well-differentiated rectal adenocarcinoma 5 cm from the anal verge, occupying less than a third of the circumference. Biopsy-proven. Endorectal ultrasound and MRI show invasion limited to the submucosa and no suspicious nodes. Which treatment is the most appropriate?
options: Abdominoperineal resection with permanent end colostomy
Neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by total mesorectal excision
Transanal fulguration of the lesion without a specimen
Transanal full-thickness local excision with negative margins
items.explanation: A small, well-differentiated T1 rectal cancer without lymphovascular invasion has a low nodal risk, so full-thickness transanal excision can cure it while preserving the sphincter. Unfavorable pathology on the specimen would prompt radical resection. Abdominoperineal resection and neoadjuvant therapy are overtreatment here. Fulguration destroys tissue without a specimen, so depth and grade cannot be confirmed.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man who has sex with men reports rectal pain, tenesmus, and bloody mucopurulent discharge for 2 weeks. Anoscopy shows friable mucosa. Nucleic acid testing identifies Chlamydia trachomatis, and serovar testing indicates lymphogranuloma venereum. What is the recommended treatment?
options: A single dose of ceftriaxone alone
Doxycycline for 3 weeks
Metronidazole for 7 days alone
Oral acyclovir for 10 days
items.explanation: Lymphogranuloma venereum proctitis is caused by invasive chlamydial serovars and needs a longer course than uncomplicated chlamydia. Doxycycline for 3 weeks is the recommended regimen, and partners are treated and tested for other infections. Ceftriaxone treats gonorrhea but not chlamydia. Metronidazole is for anaerobic or protozoal infection, and acyclovir treats herpes proctitis. Delayed treatment risks strictures and fistulas of the rectum.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with an end colostomy for rectal cancer has a symptomatic parastomal hernia 4 years later. He wants a repair that is least likely to recur. Which approach is best?
options: Primary suture repair of the fascial defect around the stoma
Local fascial repair with the stoma left in the same weakened position
Retromuscular mesh repair, with a keyhole or Sugarbaker design
Observation and a support belt as the definitive treatment
items.explanation: Primary suture repair of a parastomal hernia fails in most patients, with recurrence rates often above half. Mesh repair, using a keyhole or Sugarbaker technique, lowers recurrence, and retromuscular placement is preferred for durability. Leaving the stoma in the same weakened position invites recurrence. A support belt may relieve symptoms but does not repair the hernia.

items.stem: A 14-year-old girl has 2 days of periumbilical, then right lower quadrant pain after a viral respiratory illness. She has low-grade fever and a normal white blood cell count. CT shows several enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes in the right lower quadrant and a normal appendix. What is the best management?
options: Supportive care and observation of the self-limited illness
Urgent appendectomy to prevent perforation
Exploratory laparotomy with node biopsy
Long-term antibiotics for presumed bacterial mesenteric lymphadenitis
items.explanation: Mesenteric adenitis follows viral or Yersinia infection and mimics appendicitis, but imaging shows enlarged nodes with a normal appendix. It resolves on its own with supportive care. Appendectomy is not indicated when the appendix is normal on imaging. Exploration and node biopsy are unnecessary, and prolonged antibiotics are not needed unless a specific bacterial cause is found.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man takes aspirin and reports sudden painless maroon stool. Heart rate is 112 and blood pressure 88/54 mm Hg, improving only briefly after 2 liters of crystalloid. Hemoglobin falls from 12.1 to 8.4 g per deciliter. Upper endoscopy was normal. He continues to pass blood. What is the best next diagnostic step?
options: Elective colonoscopy after outpatient bowel preparation once he is discharged
CT angiography to localize active bleeding for embolization or surgery
Barium enema once the bleeding slows
Emergency subtotal colectomy without localizing the source
items.explanation: Ongoing hemorrhage with only a transient response to fluids needs rapid localization, and CT angiography is fast and noninvasive. It guides angioembolization or targeted resection. Delaying colonoscopy for weeks ignores an unstable bleed. A barium study cannot find an active source and obscures later endoscopy or angiography. Blind subtotal colectomy carries high mortality and is reserved for unlocalized massive bleeding.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has progressive abdominal distension. CT shows abundant low-attenuation mucinous ascites with scalloping of the liver surface and a 3 cm mucinous mass at the appendix. Cytology of the fluid shows mucin with few bland cells. What is the best treatment for pseudomyxoma peritonei in a fit patient?
options: Systemic chemotherapy alone, given for the widespread low-grade peritoneal disease
Repeated percutaneous drainage of the mucinous ascites
Cytoreductive surgery with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy
Simple appendectomy with observation of the ascites
items.explanation: Pseudomyxoma peritonei from a low-grade mucinous appendiceal neoplasm spreads along the peritoneal surfaces without invading deeply. Complete cytoreduction with intraperitoneal chemotherapy gives the best long-term control in selected patients. Systemic chemotherapy has little effect on low-grade mucinous disease. Percutaneous drainage fails because the mucin is thick, and appendectomy alone leaves widespread disease behind, so recurrence and further mucin accumulation are expected.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has a sigmoid colectomy for a T3 adenocarcinoma. Pathology reports 8 lymph nodes examined, all negative, and no other high-risk features. The tumor retained mismatch repair proteins. Which statement best describes the significance of the nodal count?
options: Fewer than 12 nodes is a high-risk feature in stage II disease and supports discussing adjuvant chemotherapy
Nodal count has no prognostic meaning once margins are negative
Eight nodes is adequate and confirms stage I disease
The nodal count only matters in rectal cancer after radiation
items.explanation: Staging accuracy depends on harvesting an adequate number of nodes, and at least 12 are recommended for colon cancer. When fewer are examined, nodal disease may be missed, so the patient is treated as high risk within stage II. Other high-risk features are T4 invasion, perforation, obstruction, lymphovascular invasion, and poor differentiation. A T3 tumor is not stage I regardless of the nodal count.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has a firm 6 cm tumor in the abdominal wall that is diagnosed as a sporadic desmoid tumor. She has no polyposis and no family history. Which genetic alteration is found in most sporadic desmoid tumors?
options: Germline mutation of the APC gene causing familial polyposis
Amplification of MDM2 in the tumor cells, as in liposarcoma
Translocation involving the SS18 gene
Activating mutation of CTNNB1, encoding beta-catenin
items.explanation: Most sporadic desmoid tumors carry a somatic CTNNB1 mutation, which stabilizes beta-catenin. Desmoids in familial adenomatous polyposis arise from germline APC mutation, which this patient lacks. MDM2 amplification characterizes well- and dedifferentiated liposarcoma, and SS18 translocation is typical of synovial sarcoma. Knowing the mutation also helps predict behavior, since some variants recur more often and may guide a choice of observation.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man has bloody diarrhea and left-sided pain on day 2 after open repair of an infrarenal aortic aneurysm. Temperature is 37.9 C, abdomen soft, and lactate normal. He is hemodynamically stable. The inferior mesenteric artery was ligated during repair. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Flexible sigmoidoscopy to grade the depth of mucosal injury
Immediate Hartmann procedure without further evaluation
Mesenteric angiography with catheter-directed thrombolysis of the colonic branches
Barium enema to outline the left colon
items.explanation: Colonic ischemia after aortic surgery is suspected here, and a stable patient without peritonitis should have endoscopy to grade the injury. Mucosal changes alone are managed with fluids, bowel rest, and antibiotics, while gangrenous mucosa calls for resection. Operating without assessment may be needless. Thrombolysis is not helpful for low-flow injury, and a barium study risks perforation in inflamed bowel.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman has no symptoms. Her father was diagnosed with colon cancer at age 55, and she has no other family history. She asks when she should begin colonoscopy. What is the best recommendation?
options: Wait until age 45 and use stool testing every 3 years
Wait until age 50 for a first colonoscopy at the usual interval
Start colonoscopy now, repeated every 5 years, because a first-degree relative was diagnosed before age 60
Begin genetic testing and avoid colonoscopy unless positive
items.explanation: A first-degree relative with colorectal cancer diagnosed before age 60 places her at increased risk, so colonoscopy should begin at 40 or 10 years before the relative's age at diagnosis, whichever is earlier, and repeat every 5 years. Waiting until 45 or 50 delays screening. Stool testing alone is less suitable for familial risk, and genetic testing does not replace endoscopy.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has 36 hours of colicky pain and vomiting. The abdomen is distended with mild right-sided tenderness. CT shows a distended, gas-filled cecum displaced to the left upper quadrant, a swirl of mesenteric vessels in the right lower abdomen, and dilated small bowel. The cecal wall enhances normally. Which operation is the best choice?
options: Colonoscopic detorsion followed by observation
Right hemicolectomy, with anastomosis if viable and stable
Detorsion with tube cecostomy alone
Cecopexy to the right lateral abdominal wall after untwisting the viable cecum
items.explanation: Cecal volvulus is an axial twist of a mobile right colon and presents as distal small bowel obstruction. Colonoscopic reduction is usually unsuccessful and recurrence is high. Cecopexy and cecostomy have higher failure and complication rates. Resection of the involved segment by right hemicolectomy is the definitive operation, and a primary anastomosis is reasonable when the tissue is viable and the patient stable.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has fever, right upper quadrant pleuritic pain, and cervical motion tenderness with purulent cervical discharge. Liver enzymes are normal and ultrasound shows a normal gallbladder and no free fluid. Which diagnosis and treatment are most appropriate?
options: Acute cholecystitis, treated with urgent cholecystectomy
Subphrenic abscess, treated with percutaneous drainage
Perforated duodenal ulcer, treated with omental patch repair
Perihepatitis from pelvic inflammatory disease, treated with antibiotics for the genital infection
items.explanation: Right upper quadrant pain with pelvic inflammatory disease signs and a normal biliary tree suggests perihepatitis, known as Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, caused by chlamydial or gonococcal spread to the liver capsule. It is treated with antibiotics for pelvic inflammatory disease. Cholecystitis would show gallbladder findings, a subphrenic abscess would show a collection, and a perforated ulcer causes free air and sudden severe pain.

items.stem: Four months after a ventral hernia repair with synthetic mesh, a 59-year-old man has a draining sinus over the incision. Wound cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. CT shows a fluid collection adjacent to the mesh with enhancement. He has had two courses of antibiotics. What is the best management?
options: Debridement and explantation of infected mesh, with staged reconstruction
A third course of oral antibiotics alone
Local wound packing and observation for a year
Injection of antibiotic directly into the sinus without any operation on the mesh
items.explanation: A chronically draining sinus with a mesh-associated collection indicates biofilm infection, which antibiotics rarely clear. Definitive management is wide debridement and removal of infected mesh, with the defect reconstructed in stages. Repeating antibiotics, packing, or local injection treats the surface only. Partial salvage is possible with some macroporous meshes, but a persistent sinus after therapy generally needs removal.

items.stem: Three months after an open inguinal hernia repair with mesh, a 49-year-old man reports burning pain and hypersensitivity to light touch over the groin, upper scrotum, and medial thigh. The repair site is intact and there is no recurrence. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Immediate mesh removal with repeat repair of the groin and nerve exploration
Opioid escalation as the long-term plan
Neuropathic medication and nerve blocks, with neurectomy reserved for failure
Observation without treatment for 2 years
items.explanation: Persistent neuralgia after groin hernia repair usually reflects injury or entrapment of the ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric, or genitofemoral nerve. Initial care is neuropathic agents and diagnostic or therapeutic nerve blocks. Surgical neurectomy, with or without mesh removal, is considered after medical treatment fails for several months. Early reoperation and long-term opioids are poor choices, and waiting years without treatment is not appropriate.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has had 6 days of right lower quadrant pain and fever. CT shows perforated appendicitis with a 4.5 cm periappendiceal abscess. She is hemodynamically stable and tolerating fluids. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Immediate open appendectomy through a right lower quadrant incision with abscess evacuation
Intravenous antibiotics alone without drainage of the abscess
Ileocecectomy with ileostomy on the day of presentation
Percutaneous drainage plus intravenous antibiotics, appendectomy decided later
items.explanation: A well-defined abscess larger than about 3 cm in a stable patient is best drained percutaneously with antibiotics, avoiding a difficult dissection through inflamed tissue. Emergency surgery in phlegmon carries higher complication and ileocecectomy risk. Antibiotics alone often fail for large abscesses. Interval appendectomy can then be discussed, and many patients recover without it. Persistent fever or an enlarging collection would prompt reassessment.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has had abdominal pain for 2 days. He is now confused, with blood pressure 82/48 mm Hg despite norepinephrine, rigid abdomen, and lactate of 6.1. CT shows free air and fluid throughout the abdomen. At laparotomy there is stool throughout the peritoneal cavity from a perforated sigmoid diverticulum. Which operation is the safest choice?
options: Laparoscopic peritoneal lavage with drain placement and broad-spectrum antibiotics alone
Sigmoid resection with end colostomy and closure of the rectal stump
Sigmoid resection with primary anastomosis and no diversion
Proximal loop colostomy leaving the perforated segment in place
items.explanation: Feculent peritonitis in a patient in shock calls for source control by resection without an anastomosis, which is the Hartmann procedure. Lavage alone does not remove the fecal source and fails in sicker patients. A primary anastomosis without diversion in a vasopressor-dependent patient risks leak and death. Diverting alone leaves a perforated segment that continues to contaminate the abdomen.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman awakens with a painful, tense blue lump at the anal verge that began 24 hours ago. She has no fever. Examination shows a 2 cm tender, discrete, dark swelling of the external anal skin with an intact, normal-appearing anal canal. What is the best treatment?
options: Excision of the thrombosed hemorrhoid under local anesthesia in 72 hours
Incision and evacuation of the clot alone, leaving the overlying skin intact
Rubber band ligation of the swelling in the office
Intravenous antibiotics and drainage in the operating room
items.explanation: A thrombosed external hemorrhoid seen within about 72 hours is best treated by excision under local anesthesia, which relieves pain faster and lowers recurrence. Simple incision leaves clot behind and often recurs. Banding is used for internal hemorrhoids and is painful on skin with somatic sensation. After 72 hours, pain usually declines and conservative care is preferred.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man completed total neoadjuvant therapy for a mid-rectal cancer and is considered for a watch-and-wait approach. Which combination of findings best supports a clinical complete response?
options: Reduction in tumor size by half on digital examination and endoscopy
A normal carcinoembryonic antigen level and no symptoms
A negative random rectal biopsy of the original tumor site
No palpable tumor, a flat white scar at endoscopy, and a clear MRI
items.explanation: Clinical complete response is judged by digital examination, proctoscopy, and MRI together, not by one test. A flat scar without ulcer or nodularity and no residual tumor on imaging support nonoperative management with tight surveillance. Partial shrinkage is not complete response. Carcinoembryonic antigen may be normal with residual tumor, and biopsies have a high false-negative rate.

items.stem: An 82-year-old man living in a long-term care facility has had 3 days of abdominal swelling and constipation. He has chronic psychiatric illness and takes anticholinergic medication. The abdomen is tympanitic but nontender. A radiograph shows a hugely dilated loop shaped like a coffee bean rising from the pelvis. There is no free air. Which initial management is appropriate?
options: Barium enema to confirm the volvulus, then observation with stool softeners alone
Endoscopic detorsion with rectal tube, then sigmoid resection this admission
Intravenous neostigmine followed by discharge on stool softeners
Immediate subtotal colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis
items.explanation: In sigmoid volvulus without peritonitis or ischemia, flexible endoscopic detorsion works in most patients and allows inspection of the mucosa. Recurrence is common, up to half, so fit patients should have sigmoid resection on the same admission. Contrast enema delays treatment, neostigmine is for pseudo-obstruction, not a twisted loop, and subtotal colectomy is excessive for a sigmoid problem.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman is on day 10 of induction chemotherapy for acute leukemia, with an absolute neutrophil count of 120 per microliter. She has fever and right lower quadrant pain. CT shows a thickened cecal wall with pericolic stranding but no free air or abscess. She is hemodynamically stable. What is the best initial management?
options: Emergency right hemicolectomy to remove the inflamed, thickened cecum at once
Laparoscopic appendectomy for presumed appendicitis
Bowel rest and antibiotics covering enteric gram-negatives and anaerobes
Outpatient oral antibiotics with a return visit in 2 weeks
items.explanation: Neutropenic enterocolitis, or typhlitis, is managed nonoperatively with bowel rest, fluids, growth factor support when indicated, and antibiotics with anaerobic coverage. Surgery is reserved for perforation, uncontrolled bleeding, or ischemia, since operating on profoundly neutropenic patients is dangerous. Appendectomy treats the wrong organ. Outpatient therapy is unsafe in a febrile neutropenic patient with bowel wall inflammation.

items.stem: After total mesorectal excision for mid-rectal cancer, which pathologic finding is the strongest predictor of local recurrence and is therefore reported by the pathologist as a key quality measure?
options: A distal margin of 3 cm from the tumor edge on the resected specimen
Mucinous histology of the primary tumor
Tumor location in the upper third of the rectum
Tumor within 1 mm of the circumferential resection margin
items.explanation: An involved circumferential resection margin, defined as tumor at or within 1 mm of the cut mesorectal surface, reflects an incomplete mesorectal plane and strongly predicts local recurrence. Distal margins of 1 to 2 cm are adequate for rectal cancer, so a 3 cm margin is not a risk. Mucinous histology carries some prognostic weight but less than margin status, and upper rectal tumors have lower local recurrence.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man has vague back pain and a 12 cm retroperitoneal mass on CT in the midline at the level of the renal hila. Serum alpha-fetoprotein and beta human chorionic gonadotropin are markedly elevated. Testicular ultrasound shows a small hypoechoic lesion. What is the best approach?
options: Percutaneous biopsy and resection of the retroperitoneal mass first
Scrotal orchiectomy followed by observation of the mass
Radical inguinal orchiectomy followed by platinum-based chemotherapy, not primary retroperitoneal resection
Radiation therapy to the retroperitoneum as definitive treatment
items.explanation: A retroperitoneal mass with elevated markers and a testicular lesion in a young man is metastatic nonseminomatous germ cell tumor. Radical inguinal orchiectomy confirms the primary and is followed by platinum-based chemotherapy, with residual mass surgery later. A scrotal approach risks altering lymphatic drainage. Biopsy and upfront resection are unnecessary, and radiation is not definitive for bulky nonseminoma.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man recovered from acute sigmoid diverticulitis with a 5 cm abscess that was drained percutaneously, and he has finished antibiotics. He feels well and has no prior colonoscopy. Which step is most appropriate in the next 6 to 8 weeks?
options: No further evaluation because CT already excluded cancer
Colonoscopy to exclude an underlying cancer and assess disease extent
Repeat CT of the abdomen in 12 months only
Contrast enema after 2 weeks to measure the length of the diseased segment
items.explanation: After complicated diverticulitis, a colonic carcinoma can mimic or coexist with the process, and CT cannot reliably exclude it. Colonoscopy after the inflammation settles, usually in 6 to 8 weeks, is recommended if the colon has not been examined recently. Repeat CT adds radiation without mucosal evaluation. A contrast enema is inferior to endoscopy and cannot allow biopsy.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a resected right colon cancer. Immunohistochemistry shows loss of MLH1 and PMS2 expression. Which test should be done next to distinguish a sporadic tumor from Lynch syndrome?
options: BRAF V600E mutation or MLH1 promoter methylation testing of the tumor
Direct sequencing of the APC gene in a blood sample
Serum carcinoembryonic antigen level
Colonoscopy of all first-degree relatives now, without any tumor testing at all
items.explanation: Loss of MLH1 and PMS2 can be caused by sporadic promoter hypermethylation or by a germline MLH1 mutation. A BRAF V600E mutation or MLH1 methylation in the tumor points to a sporadic origin, and absence of both raises the likelihood of Lynch syndrome and justifies germline testing. APC testing addresses polyposis, CEA is a monitoring marker, and relative screening does not resolve the diagnosis.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has had two recurrences of a pilonidal sinus after midline excision, each with abscess and drainage. He has hair-bearing skin in a deep natal cleft and no systemic illness. Which operation has the best chance of preventing a third recurrence?
options: Wide excision with primary midline closure
Repeat excision left open to heal by secondary intention over many weeks
Excision with off-midline flap closure to flatten the natal cleft
Phenol injection into the sinus tracts as definitive treatment
items.explanation: Recurrence in pilonidal disease is driven by the deep midline natal cleft, where moist skin and hair collect. Off-midline closure techniques, such as a Karydakis flap or cleft lift, move the incision away from the midline and flatten the cleft, lowering recurrence. Midline closure has high wound breakdown and recurrence. Open healing is slow, and phenol is an option for mild disease but not for repeated recurrence.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has leaked solid stool for 2 years since a difficult vaginal delivery was followed by a repaired tear. Fiber supplements and loperamide have helped little. Digital examination shows a weak squeeze. Which test is the most useful next step in planning surgical treatment?
options: Endoanal ultrasound for sphincter defects, with anorectal manometry
Colonoscopy alone to exclude a proximal colonic lesion as the cause of leakage
CT of the abdomen and pelvis with oral contrast
Barium enema to measure rectal capacity
items.explanation: In fecal incontinence that persists after conservative measures, the anal sphincter complex should be assessed. Endoanal ultrasound shows external and internal sphincter defects from obstetric injury, and manometry measures resting and squeeze pressures. Together they guide choice among sphincter repair, neuromodulation, and other options. Colonoscopy, CT, and barium studies do not evaluate the sphincter itself.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has Crohn disease with obstructive symptoms. CT enterography shows a 4 cm fibrotic stricture of the terminal ileum with upstream dilation and no abscess or fistula. Medical therapy has failed. Which operation is most appropriate?
options: Wide resection with 10 cm margins on both sides of disease
Limited ileocecal resection to grossly disease-free margins
Loop ileostomy diversion with no resection of the stricture
Strictureplasty across the ileocecal valve region
items.explanation: Surgery for Crohn disease conserves bowel because the disease recurs regardless of margin width. Limited ileocecal resection to grossly normal bowel is the standard for a short terminal ileal stricture. Wide margins add no benefit and risk short bowel. Diversion leaves the obstructing segment. Strictureplasty is usually used for multiple or jejunal strictures, not at the ileocecal valve.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has a painful, well-localized lump lateral to the rectus muscle, below the umbilicus. Ultrasound shows a defect in the transversus aponeurosis with bowel loops beneath an intact external oblique. Which hernia is this?
options: Direct inguinal hernia through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal
Obturator hernia through the pelvic obturator canal
Lumbar hernia through the inferior lumbar triangle
Spigelian hernia, an interparietal defect at the semilunar line
items.explanation: Spigelian hernias occur at the semilunar line, usually below the arcuate line, where the transversus aponeurosis is weak. They are interparietal, so the sac lies beneath the external oblique and the bulge can be subtle. The neck is narrow, so strangulation risk is high and repair is advised. Direct inguinal, obturator, and lumbar hernias arise at different sites.

items.stem: A 56-year-old man with ascites from cirrhosis has fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness. Paracentesis shows a neutrophil count of 1,400 per microliter, glucose of 12 mg per deciliter, protein of 2.4 g per deciliter, and ascitic lactate dehydrogenase above the serum level. Gram stain shows mixed organisms. What is the most likely diagnosis and next step?
options: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, treated with antibiotics and albumin
Secondary peritonitis, requiring imaging and surgical exploration
Tuberculous peritonitis, treated with antituberculous therapy
Hepatorenal syndrome with simple ascitic fluid
items.explanation: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis usually yields a single organism, with ascitic glucose near normal and a low lactate dehydrogenase. Very low glucose, protein above 1 g per deciliter, high lactate dehydrogenase, and polymicrobial culture point to secondary peritonitis from a gut source, which needs prompt imaging and source control. Tuberculous disease shows lymphocytes, and hepatorenal syndrome does not cause inflammatory fluid.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman has ulcerative colitis with refractory disease and wants an operation. She hopes to become pregnant within 3 years. She asks how restorative proctocolectomy may affect her plans. Which counseling is the most accurate?
options: Fertility is unchanged because the pelvic dissection spares the ovaries
Fertility improves after surgery because inflammation is eliminated
Pregnancy is contraindicated after any pouch operation for life
Fertility is reduced after pelvic pouch surgery, so subtotal colectomy with ileostomy first allows the pouch to be deferred until childbearing is complete
items.explanation: Pelvic dissection during pouch surgery causes adhesions around the tubes and reduces fecundity in women, by roughly threefold in many series. Deferring the pelvic dissection through subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy lets her control disease while preserving fertility. Pregnancy is possible after a pouch, though vaginal delivery decisions are individualized. Disease control helps conception, but the operation itself does not improve it.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman receiving clindamycin for a skin infection develops profuse diarrhea and distension, then hypotension requiring vasopressors. Temperature is 39.1 C, white blood cell count is 36,000 per microliter, and lactate is 5.8. Stool toxin testing is positive. She is already receiving oral vancomycin and intravenous metronidazole. What should be done next?
options: Sigmoid resection with Hartmann colostomy for the rectosigmoid
Continue medical therapy and add rectal enemas for 5 days
Total abdominal colectomy with end ileostomy
Loop transverse colostomy to divert the fecal stream
items.explanation: Fulminant Clostridioides difficile colitis with shock and rising lactate is lethal when surgery is delayed. Total abdominal colectomy with end ileostomy removes the diseased colon and is the standard operation. Limited resection leaves diseased bowel. Further medical therapy delays source control. A loop colostomy alone is not effective, although diverting ileostomy with colonic lavage is an emerging alternative in selected centers.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has a 1 cm right inguinal hernia found during a routine examination. It protrudes with straining, reduces easily, and causes no pain or limitation. He is otherwise healthy. Which management is the most appropriate?
options: Watchful waiting with advice on warning symptoms
Urgent repair because strangulation is likely within weeks
Truss use as the preferred long-term therapy
Bilateral exploration with mesh placement on the left
items.explanation: Randomized trials show that watchful waiting is safe for men with minimally symptomatic inguinal hernias, with a very low yearly risk of incarceration. Many eventually cross over to repair when symptoms appear, and he should return urgently for pain or irreducibility. Urgent repair is not needed. Trusses are not recommended as primary therapy, and exploring the asymptomatic opposite side is not justified.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man received radiation for prostate cancer 3 years ago. He reports recurrent bright red rectal bleeding and a hemoglobin of 9.6 g per deciliter. Colonoscopy shows rectal mucosa with telangiectasias and friability, and no mass. Which treatment is the most appropriate next step?
options: Proctectomy with coloanal anastomosis as the first-line therapy for bleeding
Mesalamine suppositories as the sole treatment
Endoscopic argon plasma coagulation of bleeding telangiectasias
A prolonged course of broad-spectrum antibiotics
items.explanation: Chronic radiation proctitis from late vascular injury is treated first with endoscopic ablation, and argon plasma coagulation controls bleeding in most patients. Major resection is a last resort because irradiated tissue heals poorly and anastomoses leak. Mesalamine has little evidence in radiation injury, and antibiotics do not treat ischemic telangiectasias because infection is not the cause.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman completed chemoradiation for a 4 cm squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal. At 8 weeks, a residual firm area remains, but it is smaller than at baseline. Biopsy is not performed. She is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate abdominoperineal resection for presumed persistent residual disease
Repeat full-dose radiation to the primary tumor
Wide local excision of the residual area right away
Continued observation, since regression may continue for up to 26 weeks
items.explanation: Squamous anal cancers can keep regressing for months after chemoradiation, and many residual areas at 8 weeks resolve by 26 weeks. A shrinking lesion in an asymptomatic patient is observed, with biopsy reserved for progression or persistence at later reassessment. Salvage abdominoperineal resection is indicated for biopsy-proven persistence or recurrence. Re-irradiation and early local excision are not standard.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man has a recurrent right inguinal hernia 3 years after an open anterior mesh repair. It is symptomatic and easily reducible. There are no signs of obstruction. Which approach is preferred for the reoperation?
options: Repeat open anterior repair through the same incision and scarred planes
A posterior preperitoneal approach through unscarred tissue planes
Primary tissue repair without any mesh
Plug and patch repair through the previous scar
items.explanation: After an open anterior repair, the anterior planes are scarred and the cord structures are at risk. A posterior approach, laparoscopic or open preperitoneal, enters virgin tissue and permits placement of a large mesh over all myopectineal orifices. The same approach in reverse applies after a posterior repair. Repeat anterior dissection and plug repair carry higher injury risk, and tissue repair has higher recurrence.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man has a draining external opening 3 cm posterior to the anal verge, off the midline to the left, after a perianal abscess drained 5 months ago. By Goodsall rule, where is the internal opening most likely located?
options: At the posterior midline, with the tract curving toward it
Directly radial at the left side of the anal canal, in line with the opening
At the anterior midline of the anal canal
Within the rectum above the anorectal ring
items.explanation: Goodsall rule predicts that an external opening behind the transverse anal line has a curved tract running to an internal opening at the posterior midline. Openings in front of the line, within about 3 cm of the verge, usually connect radially. Anterior midline and high rectal openings do not fit a posterior curved tract, and the rule is less reliable for openings farther than 3 cm from the verge.
